etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English retret, from Old French retrait or retret, from Latin retractus, from retraho. Doublet of retract, retrait, and ritratto.

definitions.definition: The act of reversing direction and receding from a forward position.
(military) Withdrawal by a military force from a dangerous position or from enemy attack.
The act of pulling back or withdrawing, as from something dangerous, or unpleasant.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: In a retreat he outruns any lackey.

definitions.definition: A peaceful, quiet place affording privacy or security.

quote.citation: 1764, Horace Walpole, The Castle of Otranto:
quote.text: " […]  But come, Lady, we are too near the mouth of the cavern; let us seek its inmost recesses.  […] " "Though all your actions are noble,  […]  is it fitting that I should accompany you alone into these perplexed retreats? Should we be found together, what would a censorious world think of my conduct?"

quote.citation: 1891, Thomas Hardy, chapter IV, in Tess of the d’Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented […], volume I, London: James R[ipley] Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., […], →OCLC, phase the first (The Maiden), pages 40–41:
quote.text: In a large bedroom upstairs, the window of which was thickly curtained with a great woollen shawl lately discarded by the landlady, Mrs. Rolliver, were gathered on this evening nearly a dozen persons, all seeking vinous bliss; all old inhabitants of the nearer end of Marlott, and frequenters of this retreat.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L'Estrange, “Fable 100: An Old Man and a Lion”, in Fables of Aesop, page 115:
quote.text: ... he built his son a house of pleasure, on purpose to keep him out of harm's way; and spared neither art nor cost to make it a delicious retreat.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “The Flower and the Leaf: Or, The Lady in the Arbour. A Vision.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: That pleasing shade they sought, a soft retreat / From sudden April showers, a shelter from the heat.

definitions.definition: (rare and obsolete, euphemistic) A peaceful, quiet place in which to urinate and defecate: an outhouse; a lavatory.
A period of retirement, seclusion, or solitude.
A period of meditation, prayer or study.

quote.citation: 2024 September, Paul Graham, “Founder Mode”, in Essays‎[1] (blog):
quote.text: For example, Steve Jobs used to run an annual retreat for what he considered the 100 most important people at Apple, and these were not the 100 people highest on the org chart.

definitions.definition: (military) A signal for a military withdrawal.
(military) A bugle call or drumbeat signaling the lowering of the flag at sunset, as on a military base.

quote.citation: 1898, Kate Douglas Wiggin, chapter 8, in Penelope’s Progress […], Boston, Mass., New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC:
quote.text: to-morrow the Royal Standard will be hoisted at Edinburgh Castle from reveille to retreat.

definitions.definition: (military) A military ceremony to lower the flag.
(chess) The move of a piece from a threatened position.
To withdraw from a position, go back.
To shrink back due to generally warmer temperatures. (of a glacier)

quote.citation: 1898, H.G. Wells, The War of the Worlds, London: William Heinemann, page 111:
quote.text: His face was a fair weakness, his chin retreated, and his hair lay in crisp, almost flaxen curls on his low forehead; his eyes were rather large, pale blue, and blankly staring.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From re- +‎ treat.
